items.title: What management is: Fayol, Taylor and Drucker
items.core_explanation_md:
**Management** can mean the **people who run an organisation** and decide, or the **activity of being in charge** of a company, department or team. It rests on **organising skills**, the skill of **getting the best out of the team** and the **principles and techniques** of organising, which **evolve** over time.

| Thinker | Contribution (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| **Henri Fayol** | Founder of **modern management methods**; **six types of organisational activities**; management is **to forecast and plan, organise, command, coordinate and control** |
| **Frederick W. Taylor** | **Scientific management** (**Taylorism**): analysing and synthesising **workflows** to improve **efficiency and labour productivity**; book of **1911**, voted in **2001** by the Academy of Management Fellows as the **most influential management book of the 20th century** |
| **Peter Drucker** | Called Taylor the **first person in recorded history to study work systematically** |

Management is **not just common sense**: it is a **discipline, a culture and an art and science**, and the **effectiveness of an organisation reflects the quality of its management**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Fayol's verbs (forecast and plan, organise, command, coordinate, control) anticipate the later list of planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling.

items.title: The management process and its five functions
items.core_explanation_md:
The **management process** is a **continuous social process** of co-operation and relationships, split into **five connected functions** that matter to every organisation, **whatever its size, ownership or type**.

| Function | Core task |
| --- | --- |
| **Planning** | **Decide in advance** what, when, where, how and by whom, in line with the **objectives**; helps manage change and monitor progress; **influences all other functions** |
| **Organising** | **Task management** (who does what, how tasks are grouped), the **reporting structure** and **decision making** (at what level) |
| **Staffing** | **Recruitment, selection, training, development, motivation, pay, job rotation, enrichment, transfers, termination, retirement** |
| **Directing** | **Leadership, motivation, communication, supervision** |
| **Controlling** | **Standards, measurement, comparison, corrective action**; **variance analysis** |

**Controlling in four steps:** (a) **establish performance standards**; (b) **measure actual performance**; (c) **compare** it with the standards; (d) **take corrective action**. Good control is **always preceded by good planning**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Controlling needs the standards set in planning; without a plan there is nothing to compare actual results with.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the four steps of controlling?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Establish standards, measure actual performance, compare it with the standards, and take corrective action.

items.title: The four elements of directing
items.core_explanation_md:
**Directing** is guiding and supervising subordinates. It is **not enough to recruit and place people**; they must be **directed** to achieve organisational goals.

| Element | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Leadership** | **Influencing a person's or group's actions** to meet the desired goals; the quality of leadership is the **foundation of a manager's success** |
| **Motivation** | **Inspiring and encouraging** people through **healthy, pleasant surroundings** and **incentives** |
| **Communication** | **Speedy, clear two-way flow**: instructions down, information and suggestions up |
| **Supervision** | **Continuous monitoring** so that **quality** and **targets** are met **in time** and **to the laid-down norms** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Telling subordinates what to do is not enough; supervision checks that it is done properly and on time.

items.core_explanation_md:

items.title: Maslow, McGregor and Herzberg
items.core_explanation_md:
**Maslow's hierarchy of needs (five levels, lowest to highest):** **physiological**, **safety**, **love and belongingness**, **self-esteem**, **self-actualisation**. **Only unsatisfied needs influence behaviour**; a person moves up **only after the lower need is at least minimally satisfied**.

| McGregor | Assumption |
| --- | --- |
| **Theory X** | People are **lazy**, **dislike work**, **avoid responsibility**, **want direction and security**, **lack creativity** and **resist change**: they need **close supervision and coercion** |
| **Theory Y** | Work is **as natural as play**; people are **self-directed** and **self-controlled** when motivated, **creative**, and **passive only because of experience in organisations** |

**Herzberg's two-factor theory:**

- **Motivators** (**challenging work, recognition, responsibility**) give **positive satisfaction**.
- **Hygiene factors** (**status, job security, salary, fringe benefits**) **do not motivate if present** but **demotivate if absent**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Salary is a hygiene factor in Herzberg's theory: its absence upsets staff, but raising it does not by itself motivate.

self_check.prompt_text: Under Herzberg's theory, is salary a motivator or a hygiene factor?

items.title: Quantitative, systems and contingency schools
items.core_explanation_md:
| School | Core idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Quantitative (management science)** | After **World War II**; **mathematical and statistical models** solve managerial problems; emphasis on **operations** and **management information systems**; builds **models and hypotheses**, collects **data**, **experiments**, develops **quantitative techniques** |
| **Systems** (Katz and von Bertalanffy) | The organisation is an **open system** that **interacts with its environment** to get resources; both the **environment and internal conditions** matter |
| **Contingency** | **No single best way** to manage; it **depends on internal and external circumstances**; criticised as **reactive** and for lacking **standard principles** |

**Leadership studies (1950s) in the contingency school:**

| Ohio State University | University of Michigan Survey Research Centre |
| --- | --- |
| **Consideration**: rapport, relationships, **concern for people** | **Relation-oriented**: social interaction, **mutual respect and trust**, **empowering people** |
| **Initiating structure**: **structure, scheduling, roles, task completion** | **Task-oriented**: **structure, planning, priorities, rewards and punishments** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: A bank, for example, is an open system: customers and regulators react to its products and services.

self_check.prompt_text: What does the contingency school say about the best way to manage?
self_check.expected_takeaway: There is no unique best way; it depends on the internal and external situation.

items.title: The learning organisation and Senge's five disciplines
items.core_explanation_md:
A **learning organisation** is one where **all employees identify and solve problems** and **continuously enhance their capacity to learn and grow**. It is organised around **problem solving**, **teamwork**, **empowered employees** and an **open information system**, not around efficiency alone. The idea spread in the **1990s**.

**Peter Senge** (*The Fifth Discipline*): organisations where people **continually expand their capacity to create the results they truly desire**.

| Discipline | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Personal mastery** | Developing the capacity to achieve **personal goals**; the **cornerstone** |
| **Shared vision** | **Collaboration** and a **joint vision**, not mere compliance with orders |
| **Mental models** | Understanding the **assumptions and generalisations** we hold; **reflection** on what we perceive versus what happened |
| **Team learning** | **Humility** and willingness to consider **others' views** |
| **Systems thinking** | Seeing everything as **interrelated and interconnected** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Benefits listed by the courseware: staying ahead of competitors, higher effectiveness, productivity and output, and a better image.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of Senge's disciplines is the cornerstone?

items.core_explanation_md:
A **business model** covers the **operational characteristics and key structural features** of a business. The courseware gives these examples:

| Model | Idea | Examples |

| **Profit pyramid** | **Low-priced** products first, then **expensive** ones with **higher margins** | **General Motors** |
| **Multi-component systems** | **Cheap razors or printers**, profit from **blades or cartridges** | **Gillette, HP** |
| **Advertisement** | **Basic product free**, money from **advertising** | **YouTube, Google** |
| **Switchboard** | **Intermediary** connecting **many sellers and buyers** | **eBay, Amazon, Flipkart** |
| **Time** | A **pioneer** with new research succeeds until **competitors join** | pioneers |
| **Efficiency** | **Standardised, low-cost, low-margin, mass appeal** | **Southwest Airlines, Wal-Mart, Dell** |
| **Blockbuster** | Few **star products** under **patent protection** | **Pharma, film** |
| **Profit multiplier** | A concept **reused across products** through **synergy** | **Walt Disney** |
| **Entrepreneurial** | **Specialised products** not attractive to large firms | **Tata acquiring 1MG** |
| **De facto industry standard** | **Free or very low cost** products to become the **standard**, then **high-end products** | **Microsoft** |

items.title: Information explosion, managing change, globalisation and sustainability
items.core_explanation_md:
**Information explosion:** huge growth in digital data makes **storage, retrieval and processing** harder, but gives an **edge** to organisations that exploit it; the **digital gap** can create **inequalities**; **privacy** and **misinformation** are issues.

**Managing change:** people prefer **comfort zones** and resist new technology, learning and training; the manager must make change **smooth without hurting productivity and profit**. **New products and services** need **customer feedback and research** and careful development and testing. **Technological change** (such as fintech) disrupts banking. **Employee management** and loyalty matter.

**Globalisation:** **more export, sourcing, joint ventures and foreign borrowing**; but more **emissions from transport of goods**, **economic specialisation**, **overuse of natural resources** and **reduced biodiversity**.

**Environmental sustainability:** the **UN's 17 sustainable development goals**: **no poverty, zero hunger, good health, quality education, gender equality, clean water, affordable clean energy, decent work and growth, industry, innovation and infrastructure, reduced inequalities, sustainable cities, responsible consumption and production, climate action, life below water, life on land, peace and justice, partnerships.**
items.expanded_explanation_md: Management must balance sustainability expectations with business goals when it makes decisions.

items.title: Strategy, plan and strategic management
items.core_explanation_md:
**Strategy** comes from the Greek **strategos**, "the general's views". It is the **pattern of decisions** that shows a company's **objectives, policies, businesses, and the kind of organisation** it intends to be. A strategy combines **mission** (core purpose), **vision** (future direction), **clientele**, **resources** and **present and future**.

**Strategic management** covers the decisions and actions that decide **long-term performance**: **scanning** the external and internal environment, **formulating** long-term plans, **implementing** them and **evaluating and controlling** them.

| | **Plan** | **Strategy** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nature** | **Concrete**, a programme or scheme for a definite purpose | A **blueprint or idea** to reach a goal |
| **Deviation** | **Does not allow** deviation (if Plan A fails, move to Plan B) | **Flexible**, open to **adaptation and change** |
| **Style** | Useful when being **organised and on track** matters | Useful when **creativity, collaboration and innovation** matter; encourages **debate** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: A plan is a fixed route; a strategy keeps the destination but lets the route change.

self_check.prompt_text: Which is flexible and open to change, a plan or a strategy?

items.title: Types and elements of strategy, and SWOT
items.core_explanation_md:
**Three types** (a business may use all at once):

| Type | Level | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Corporate strategy** | Overall direction and **portfolio of businesses**: **stability, growth, retrenchment** | TCS selling a **marginally profitable** software business (retrenchment) |
| **Business strategy** | **Business unit or product**: **competitive** or **cooperative** | An **alliance** with another company |
| **Functional strategy** | **Functional areas** (R and D, technology, marketing): maximise **productivity of resources** | Advertising or imitating rivals' products |

**Four elements of strategic management:**

1. **Environmental scanning** (the context): **monitoring and evaluating internal and external information**; **SWOT** = **Strengths and Weaknesses** (internal, controllable by top management in the short run) and **Opportunities and Threats** (external, mostly outside its control).
2. **Strategy formulation**: set **direction** through **mission and vision** and choose **corporate, business and functional** strategies.
3. **Strategy implementation**: **what, when, where and by whom**, keeping decisions **consistent with the strategy**.
4. **Strategy evaluation and control**: **feedback and corrective action**, because success today does not guarantee success tomorrow.
items.expanded_explanation_md: SWOT separates what the organisation can change (strengths and weaknesses) from what it can only respond to (opportunities and threats).

items.title: Vision, mission and the phases of strategic management
items.core_explanation_md:
| | **Vision** | **Mission** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Question** | "**What do we want to become?**" | **Why do we exist?** |
| **Nature** | **Forward looking**, ideally **one short sentence**, the **foundation** of the mission | A statement of **purpose, philosophy, beliefs and business principles**: its **contribution to society** |
| **Content** | A leap of faith that gives energy | Covers **customers, products or services, markets, technology, survival, growth and profitability, philosophy, self-concept, public image, employees** |

**Four phases of strategic management** (pioneered by **General Electric** and the **Boston Consulting Group**):

1. **Basic financial (budgetary) planning**: **annual** budget from **internal** data.
2. **Forecast-based planning**: **three to five years**, using **extrapolation** and external data.
3. **Externally oriented (strategic) planning**: **top-down**, led by key managers with **external consultants**, typically **five years**.
4. **Strategic management**: an **integrated plan** with **all managers**, **shorter review cycles**, **contingencies** and a **broader, more interactive** process.

**Benefits:** a **clearer strategic vision**, **focus on strategically important issues**, a **better understanding of the dynamic environment**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Strategic planning moved from a top-down exercise to strategic management as more managers were involved and plans were reviewed more often.

items.title: Business environment analysis
items.core_explanation_md:
A business **does not operate in isolation**. It must understand the environment around it: **suppliers, customers, competitors**, **technology**, the **ecological and social environment**, **regulatory, political, cultural and demographic** factors.

- Exceptional shocks (wars, earthquakes, terror attacks) are rare, but ordinary uncertainties (**technology, regulation, demographics, markets**) are constant.
- Managers who **understand the external environment** can **prepare for contingencies**.
- **SWOT analysis** is a basic way of scanning it.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware describes the operating environment as including suppliers, customers and competitors, which can change quickly.

self_check.expected_takeaway: For example technology and regulation (also political, cultural, demographic and ecological factors).

items.title: What planning is
items.core_explanation_md:
**Planning** is **thoughtful discussion and deliberate contemplation before a task**, so that the organisation is ready with an **execution and implementation plan** and saves **effort and time**. It involves an **objective analysis of future requirements** and the **orderly series of actions** expected to achieve the goals.

**Planning covers:** **what** is to be done, **where**, **how**, **when** and **who** will execute.

It weighs **every conceivable risk** (losses, defections). Decisions and **directional plans** (**strategic, tactical, operational**) rest on **finances, time frame, infrastructure and resources**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware describes planning as the foundation for every other function of management.

self_check.expected_takeaway: What is to be done, where, how, when and who will execute.

items.title: Steps in the planning process
items.core_explanation_md:
The courseware lists **eight steps**:

| Step | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 1. **Opportunity analysis** | Understand the **opportunity** and its prospects: the basis for the plans |
| 2. **Objective establishment** | **Objectives first**: no strategy can be built without them |
| 3. **Developing planning premises** | **Forecast-based assumptions** from a **realistic assessment of the environment**; covers **forecasting, basic policies, existing plans**; kept **monitored and upgraded** |
| 4. **Alternatives identification** | A **written record** of alternative means, narrowed to the **most attractive** |
| 5. **Evaluating alternatives** | Examine **strong and weak points**; use **statistical methods and computers** |
| 6. **Selecting the best alternative** | Decide whether the **initial plan or an alternative** is more effective |
| 7. **Formulating derivative plans** | **Sub or secondary plans**: new **policies and procedures**, **coordination**, working to the **main plan's targets** |
| 8. **Follow-up and review** | Planning is **continuous**: monitor and **adjust** the plans |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Derivative plans turn the chosen plan into detailed actions for each unit.

items.title: Advantages of planning
items.core_explanation_md:
**Main advantages (courseware):**

1. **Coordination of various activities**: efforts of departments are directed to the goals set in the plan.
2. **Optimisation of resources**: activities with the **maximum demand for resources** get the **optimum allocation** for the **maximum return on investment**.
3. **Inspirations and responsibilities**: staff know the **commonly expected accomplishments** and the **risk is lessened**.
4. **Establishment of execution principles**: **milestones** mark progress and show whether things are **moving as planned**.
5. **Adaptability**: the guiding principles can **adjust to change**.

**Other advantages listed:** **reduces uncertainty**, is **focused on objectives**, **facilitates control**, **encourages creativity and innovation**, **anticipates problems and copes with change**, **limits vulnerabilities**, supports **morale**, helps **economies**, gives managers the **upper hand** and **empowers development**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Milestones turn a long-range plan into checkpoints against which progress can be measured.

self_check.prompt_text: What do milestones in a plan help managers decide?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Whether things are moving as planned and, if not, what adjustments are necessary.

items.title: Disadvantages of planning
items.core_explanation_md:
Planning can **harm** an organisation if it is **not carried out as intended**.

| Disadvantage | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Forestalls activity** | Managers may be so absorbed in planning that they **have no time to act** ("**death by plan**") |
| **Lack of concern** | Strong systems may make managers **assume all is well**, so they **fail to monitor progress** or notice **external shifts** |
| **Forestalls adaptability** | Lower-level supervisors may **stick to the plan** even if it is **not working** |
| **Hinders innovativeness** | People think they must **only carry out the plan**, which **stifles creativity** |

**Others:** planning takes **time**, may rest on **unreliable data**, can be **expensive**, causes **rigidity**, can give a **false sense of security**, may be bent to **participants' interests**, and a **fast-changing environment** makes it harder.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The cure for these problems is to review and revise plans continuously instead of treating them as final.

self_check.prompt_text: What is meant by "death by plan"?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Planning so much that no time is left to carry out the plans (forestalls activity).

items.title: PESTLE analysis
items.core_explanation_md:
**PESTLE** evaluates the **business environment** and its likely impact on performance, to develop **strategies and plans**.

| Letter | Factor | Banking illustration (courseware) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **P** | **Political** | **Government laws** affect banking; the sector is **open to political influence** |
| **E** | **Economic** | **Interest rates, inflation, exchange rates, unemployment**; a **recession** reduces capital banks can access |
| **S** | **Social (socio-cultural)** | **Languages, demographics, attitudes**; consumers want a **seamless banking experience** |
| **T** | **Technological** | The **Internet** changes products and **speeds distribution** and lowers **communication cost** |
| **L** | **Legal** | **Privacy, consumer and trade laws**; **regulatory compliance costs** |
| **E** | **Environmental** | **Mobile banking** cuts **paper use** and **branch visits** |

**Three steps:** **identify** the relevance of each factor, **collect and categorise** information, **analyse** the data and **draw conclusions**.

**Note:** the courseware once calls the PESTLE factors "internal", but all six are **external** factors; they are taught here as external.

**Advantages:** **cost effective**, **easy framework**, **deep understanding**, **development alertness**, **opportunity exploitation**.

items.title: Objectives, planning premises, evaluating alternatives and finalising the plan
items.core_explanation_md:
**Fixation of objectives:** planning **begins with objectives**: first for the **organisation as a whole**, then for each **subordinate work unit**; departmental goals take **direction from the overarching goals**.

**Planning premises** are the **assumed conditions** on which planning is based: **population trends**, **political and economic climate**, **cost of production**, **advertising policy**, availability of **labour, material and electricity**. A **forecast** is a prediction about the future. Premises typically rest on expectations about **product demand**, **production volume**, **expenses and price**, **labour and material availability**, **government economic policy**, **customer preferences**, **new technology** and **sources of funds**.

**Criteria for evaluating alternatives:** **cost, profitability, break-even point**; **market, sales potential, competitor reaction**; **ability to meet corporate objectives**; **strengths and weaknesses**; **timing**; **intuition about success**.

**Finalising the plan:** an **action plan** that answers: **what steps**, **who** will do the work, **how long**, **where**, and **how** it will be completed.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The action plan turns the chosen alternative into assignments, times and places.

items.title: Forecasting: long, medium and short term
items.core_explanation_md:
**Forecasting** is **predicting the future from evidence of the past and the present**. It boosts management's **confidence** but cannot remove the **unpredictability** of the future; prediction is the **foundation for premises** and uses **statistical analysis**.

| Type | Period and use | Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Long term** | Typically **3 to 5 years**; funding needs and **investable surplus** | **Asset management**, **systematic leveraging and deleveraging**, **cash reserves** build earnings, **variance evaluation** | **Unpredictable economy**, **no historical data**, **limited technology**, **silent data** |
| **Medium term** | **Relatively minor strategic decisions**; basis of **operational and business budgets** | | |
| **Short term** | **Less than one year**, typically **1 to 6 months** | **Less time and money**; shows the **current finances**; **scenario analysis** for preventive action | **High starting cost**, **complex payables and receivables**, need for **granular precision**, **late decisions** |

**Forecasting process:** **identify and develop the structure** (the **strategic factors** that materially affect the forecast); **estimate the future course of business** using **statistical and other techniques**; **analyse deviations in previous forecasts** to improve the procedure.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Reviewing past forecast errors is how a forecasting process gets better over time.

items.title: Decision making: groups, conditions and principles
items.core_explanation_md:
**Decision making** is the **selection of one course of action from several alternatives**. It is a **prominent function of management**, **not confined to planning**, and should be a **rational process** based on **systematic analysis of all relevant facts**, not intuition.

**Hierarchy:** **top management** takes **crucial and strategic** decisions and sets **broad policies**; **routine** decisions are **delegated** to middle and lower management.

| **Group decisions** | |
| --- | --- |
| **Advantages** | **Thorough evaluation**; **easier implementation** (a feeling of involvement); **enhanced team spirit** |
| **Disadvantages** | **Time consuming and costly**; **disagreements and indecision** (conflict, blame-games, no unanimity); **no participation or domination** (members shirk responsibility or one member dominates) |

**Conditions of decision making:**

| Condition | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Certainty** | The decision maker **knows exactly what will happen** |
| **Risk** | Information is **partial**, so **probabilities** are assigned: **objective** (from **past experience**) or **subjective** (from **intuition**) |
| **Uncertainty** | **Probabilities cannot be assigned**; the **likelihood cannot be measured** |

items.title: Why organisation is important
items.core_explanation_md:
The departments must **communicate and coordinate**; organising sets the **channels of communication** and brings **resources together** towards one goal.

| Factor | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Efficiency in administration** | **Collapsing comparable jobs** into one area of expertise; **integration** of effort; shows **activities and authority links** between departments |
| **Resource optimisation** | Each worker has a **role that fits**, reducing **misunderstanding, delay, duplication and overlap** |
| **Gaining expertise** | **Division of labour** completes the **most work in the shortest time** while retaining the benefit of **experience** |
| **Promoting effective communication** | **Channels** between functions and positions |
| **Creating transparency** | The **job description** states **tasks, duties and responsibilities** in writing, with **power and responsibility** assigned |
| **Expansion and development** | Full use of resources and **appropriate division of labour** lets management **expand methodically** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Transparency comes from the written job description, which is also the base for assigning duties.

items.title: Principles of organising
items.core_explanation_md:
**Fourteen principles listed:** **objectives, specialisation, coordination, authority, responsibility, span of control, balance, continuity, unity of direction, unity of command, exception, simplicity, efficiency, scalar principle.**

| Principle | Meaning (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| **Work specialisation** | Breaking tasks into **distinct jobs**; **division of labour**; **too much** isolates staff and creates **dependence**, so firms use **job rotation** and expanded jobs |
| **Authority** | **Legitimate power** to **decide, issue orders and allocate resources**; the **chain of command** starts at the **top** |
| **Chain of command** | **Continuous line of authority** from the top to **every individual**; rests on the **scalar principle** and **unity of command** |
| **Unity of command** | **One manager** for each worker, to avoid **confusion from competing demands** |
| **Scalar principle** | A **transparent chain** from the top to everyone; **gang plank**: a subordinate may contact a **superior's superior in an emergency**, with immediate superiors briefed |
| **Delegation** | **Passing on responsibilities or authority** to subordinates; a manager **cannot delegate authority he does not have** |
| **Span of control** | **Number of people reporting directly** to a manager; **wide** span = more independence for subordinates; **narrow** span = **more time with direct reports** and **professional growth** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Unity of command and the scalar principle are the two guiding principles behind the chain of command.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Each worker has only one manager or supervisor to whom he or she is directly accountable.

items.core_explanation_md:
A **modification of the line organisation**: **staff supervisors and specialists** are attached to the line to give **special and auxiliary support**. **Line executives hold the authority of command**; **staff have an advisory role** (advise, guide, counsel). **Two channels of authority** flow together: **line authority** and **staff authority**.

**Staff types:** **staff assistants** (for example a personal assistant to the managing director, the marketing manager's secretary) and **staff specialists** (operations control manager, quality controller, PRO).

| **Advantages** | **Disadvantages** |
| --- | --- |
| **Relief to line executives** | A **fundamental misunderstanding**: confusion between line and staff authority |
| **Professional counsel** | **Lack of reliable guidance** (second-hand experience) |
| **Benefits of specialisation** | **Conflicts** between line and staff |
| **Better coordination** | **Expense**: high pay for staff experts |
| **Research and development** | **Assumption of authority**: staff resented by line |
| **Training** | **Staff steals the show**: line feels credit goes to experts |
| **Balanced decisions**, **unity of action** | |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The key risk is confusion over who has the authority to command and who only advises.

self_check.prompt_text: Who holds the authority of command in a line and staff organisation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Line executives; staff members have only advisory roles.

items.title: Functional and committee organisation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Functional organisation:** **specialists** hold positions at the highest levels and each functional area (operations, finance, marketing, personnel) is under **specialists with authority over that function wherever it is carried out**. **Three authorities:** **line, staff and function**. **Subordinates receive commands from several specialists**, so **unity of command does not apply**. The courseware credits **F. W. Taylor** with the idea.

| | **Advantages** | **Disadvantages** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Functional** | **Specialisation**, **efficient control**, **efficiency**, **cost effectiveness**, **expansion** | **Confusion**, **lack of coordination** (weak discipline because many people control a worker), **hard to fix accountability**, **conflicts among equal supervisors**, **expense** |
| **Committee** (a group with various knowledge solving organisation-wide issues) | **Better quality of decisions**; **goals, plans and policies**; **participation**; **less prejudice and conflict**; **complicated problems**; **commitment**; **sharing of authority** | **Conflict**; **delay**; **diversion**; **the shifting tendency** (deferring decisions to committees); **lack of secrecy**; **distributed responsibility**; **division of accountability** (no one is held responsible) |
items.expanded_explanation_md: In a committee decision, everyone is responsible, so in practice no single person is held accountable.

self_check.prompt_text: Does the principle of unity of command apply in a functional organisation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; subordinates take orders from several specialists.

items.title: Formal and informal organisation
items.core_explanation_md:
| | **Formal organisation** (open or overt) | **Informal organisation** (hidden or covert) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Contents** | **Goals and objectives, policies and procedures, job descriptions, financial resources, authority structures, channels of communication, products and services** | **Beliefs and assumptions, perceptions and attitudes, values, feelings, group norms** |
| **Origin** | Created by managers through **organising** | Forms **naturally** from **social and friendly groups** inside the formal structure |
| **Purpose** | **Methodical work** and organisational goals | **Psychological fulfilment** |
| **Chain of command** | **Defined**: hierarchical | **None**; the source of information **cannot be traced** |
| **Advantages** | **Organised tasks**; **objectives achieved**; **no duplication**; **harmony**; **place in chain of command**; **emphasis on work** | **Fast communication**; **satisfies social needs**; **correct response** (managers learn real views); **a strategic tool** (the **grapevine**) |
| **Disadvantages** | **Postpones action** (scalar chain); **ignores social needs**; **only work matters** | **Rumour spreading**; **no organised tasks**; **may oppose management decisions**; **stresses individual interests** |

The **informal structure depends on the formal structure**: no job positions, no informal groups.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Managers can use the informal organisation, for example the grapevine, to communicate quickly and win support.

items.title: Organisation charts and manuals
items.core_explanation_md:
An **organisation chart** is a **diagram** of the **primary functions**, how they relate, the **formal channels of power** and **each manager's authority** (George R. Terry: a graphical form of key functions, relationships and channels of supervision).

| Classification | Types |
| --- | --- |
| **By content** | **Master charts** (the **whole formal structure**) and **supplementary charts** (**linkages, authorities and responsibilities** in one department) |
| **By preparation** | **Vertical (top-down)**: hierarchy as a pyramid, highest at the top; **horizontal (left to right)**: levels from left to right, **clear mental picture of levels**, shows **length of authority chain**; **circular**: **concentric circles** with the **top at the centre**, but it **often confuses** |

**Organisation manual:** a **compact book** of the **aims**, **authority and responsibilities of positions** and **processes and procedures**. **Four sections:** **policy manual, operational manual, organisational manual, rules and regulations manual**.

| | Chart and manual | Manual alone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Advantages** | **Management tool**; **avoid overlap and duplication**; **resolve conflicts**; **training guides**; **reference for outsiders** | **Quick learning** of procedures; **simple instructions** |
| **Disadvantages** | **Rigidity**; **partial picture** (formal patterns only); **inadequate description** of authority; **psychological issues** (superiority or inferiority) | **Costly and time-consuming**; **little room for initiative** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: A chart shows who reports to whom; a manual adds the policies, procedures and job details that a chart cannot show.

items.title: Organisational culture and its four types
items.core_explanation_md:
**Organisational culture** is the **values, attitudes, beliefs and behaviours** that give an organisation its **one-of-a-kind social and emotional work environment**. It is **one of the hardest things to change** because it grows from **written and unwritten rules** developed over time. **Every organisation has a culture**, whether or not it was cultivated on purpose.

**Culture profile dimensions:** **innovative, aggressive, result-oriented, stable, people or team oriented, detail-oriented.**

| Type | Core idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Clan** | Built on **working together**; members feel like a **family**; leadership is **mentoring** |
| **Adhocracy** | **Energy and inventiveness**; **innovative and entrepreneurial**; **calculated risks**; **individual ingenuity and freedom** |
| **Market** | **Competitive**; **focus on goals**; **strict and demanding leaders**; **market share and profitability** decide value |
| **Hierarchy** | **Hierarchy and control**; **formal**, **stringent protocols**; **productivity and predictability** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The four types show how much an organisation prizes teamwork, innovation, competition or control.

self_check.prompt_text: Which culture is built on hierarchy and control and values productivity and predictability?

items.title: Authority and responsibility
items.core_explanation_md:
| | **Authority** | **Responsibility** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Meaning** | **Formal, institutional or legal power** to carry out the job's responsibilities; the **right to give orders** | **Obligation** of a subordinate to complete delegated tasks; a **moral commitment** |
| **Direction** | **Downward**, superior to subordinate | **Upward**, subordinate to superior |
| **Delegation** | **Can be delegated** | **Cannot be delegated** or **transferred horizontally** |

A superior can delegate authority but **cannot absolve himself of responsibility**; **equal authority should accompany responsibility**.

**Sources of authority:**

| Source | Basis |
| --- | --- |
| **Legitimate** | The **status quo** and cultural system of rights and obligations |
| **Coercive** | The **ability to instil fear** |
| **Rewarding** | The **ability to reward** (for example granting paid vacations) |
| **Expertise** | **Knowledge and ability** in a field |
| **Referent** | **Faith in, admiration of and imitation** of a leader |

**Characteristics of authority:** the **foundation for getting things done**; **legitimacy**; **decision making**; **subjectivity in implementation**.

**Forms of responsibility:** **operating responsibility** (accountable for one's own actions at work) and **ultimate responsibility** (the manager answers for the work being done effectively).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The ultimate accountability stays with the manager even after tasks are delegated.

self_check.prompt_text: Can responsibility be delegated?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; authority can be delegated, but responsibility cannot be passed on or transferred horizontally.

items.title: Organisational change and resistance to it
items.core_explanation_md:
**Organisational change** is the actions a company takes to **modify a significant aspect** of itself (culture, technology, infrastructure). Managing it typically involves **three steps: planning, implementation and follow-up**.

**Drivers:** **new management**, **changes in team structure**, **new technologies**, **new business models**.

| Category | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Developmental** | **Improvement** of **existing** processes and procedures |
| **Changes during transition** | Moving to a **new state**, such as a **merger or acquisition** or **automating a task** |
| **Transformational** | **Drastic, fundamental** change in the **way of doing business**; the **final effect is unknown** (for example entering **new product categories or niches**) |

**Change management** is a **methodical, systematic** strategy to address the transition of objectives, procedures or technologies. Each change request is judged for its effect on **scope, timing, cost, quality, human resources, communications, risk and recovery**.

**Resistance to change** is **rejecting or fighting changes** that disturb the status quo, shown **directly or indirectly**, **organised or personal**. **Signs:** **fault finding**, **nit-picking**, **offensive remarks**, **absence from meetings**, **dishonoured commitments**, **continuous arguments**, **disruptive behaviour**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: An early check of each change request against scope, time, cost and quality avoids cascading problems.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the three types of organisational change.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Developmental change, change during transition and transformational change.

items.title: Seven change management models
items.core_explanation_md:
| Model | Originator | Core idea |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Lewin's model** | **Kurt Lewin** | **Unfreeze** (prepare, overcome the status quo), **change** (the transformation; needs strong leadership, communication, scheduling), **refreeze** (make the new state stable and routine) |
| **McKinsey 7S** | **McKinsey and Company, late 1970s** | **Strategy, structure, systems, shared values, style, staff, skills**: all seven are **interconnected** and equally important; failure of one can fail the whole |
| **Kotter's eight stages** | **John P. Kotter** | **Rising sense of urgency**; **putting together the team**; **getting the vision right**; **communicating**; **getting things off the ground** (empower action); **concentrating on near-term goals**; **not giving up**; **adapting to new circumstances** (make change part of the culture) |
| **Nudge theory** | **Cass Sunstein and Richard Thaler** | **Gently nudge** people and **encourage and motivate** them to change |
| **ADKAR** | | **A**wareness (courseware: Consciousness), **D**esire, **K**nowledge, **A**bility (Capability), **R**einforcement, obtained **in order** |
| **Bridges' transition model** | **William Bridges** | **Transition**, unlike change, happens **from the inside out**: **end (give up and let go)**, **neutral zone**, **new beginning** |
| **Kubler-Ross five stages** | **Elizabeth Kubler-Ross** | The **grief model**: **denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 7S weakness is that every element depends on the others, so one failure breaks the whole model.

items.title: Conflict dynamics, conflict management and resolution
items.core_explanation_md:
**Conflict dynamics:** the stages of a conflict **change the environment** in which the parties interact.

**Conflict management** balances **minimising negative outcomes** and **maximising positive outcomes**; it needs **negotiating, creative thinking and a range of strategies** matched to the context. Its goal is better **learning and group outcomes**, such as organisational **efficiency or performance**.

**Skills needed:** **clear and effective communication**, **attentive listening**, **empathy**, **problem solving**, **positive attitude**, **setting priority levels**, **patience**, **reading body language**.

**Five strategies for conflict resolution:**

1. **Refrain from ignoring the conflict**: ignored conflicts **worsen** and **resurface**.
2. **Explain the nature of the issue**: **gather information**, **find the real issue** with everyone affected, act as an **impartial mediator**.
3. **Organise a meeting** of the parties in an **impartial atmosphere**.
4. **Identify a solution**: **negotiate** and **collaborate on a detailed plan of action**.
5. **Maintain vigilance and follow up**: **check** the issue was resolved and **continue the dialogue** if the solution is not working.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Follow-up matters because a resolved conflict may return if the agreed steps are not carried out.

items.title: What staffing is: functions and objectives
items.core_explanation_md:
**Staffing** is **recruiting and developing the people** needed to fill an organisation's roles. It covers **personnel planning, procurement (selection and placement), training and development, performance evaluation and compensation**.

**Functions:** obtain **qualified people** for positions; select the **most qualified candidates** (higher productivity); use human resources **effectively**; raise **job satisfaction and morale**; secure the organisation's **continued existence and expansion**; put people in the **right jobs**.

**Objectives:** **right people for the right positions**; **educate and cultivate** human resources; design **policies on transfer and promotion**; **motivate** towards better performance; build **positive employer-employee relations**; meet workers' demands so they are **loyal**; keep **morale** strong.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware cites Drucker: of all the resources accessible to man, only man can grow and develop.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two objectives of staffing.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example the right employees for the right positions, and developing human resources.

items.title: Nature and salient features of staffing
items.core_explanation_md:
**Nature (courseware):** **concentrated on individuals**; **development oriented**; **all-pervasive** (every business and level); **an ongoing procedure**; has **human objectives**; serves **individuals and groups**; creates an **environment for productive work**; **multidisciplinary** (sociology, anthropology, management, psychology: "**human engineering**"); an **essential part of general management**; a **blend of art and science**.

**Salient features:** **involves human beings**; a **distinct managerial function**; **needed at all managerial levels** (managers stay **ultimately responsible** for hiring decisions even with a personnel department); linked to **social responsibility**; influenced by the **internal** environment (promotion, demotion and transfer policies) and the **external** one (**government policy**, the **educational environment**).
items.expanded_explanation_md: A personnel department helps managers but does not remove their duty to staff their own teams.

self_check.prompt_text: Who remains ultimately responsible for staffing decisions in a department?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The responsible manager, even where a personnel department exists.

items.title: Facets and significance of staffing
items.core_explanation_md:
**Three facets:**

| Facet | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Recruitment** | A **positive process** that attracts **more suitable people to apply** |
| **Selection** | Reviews applications and **chooses the best fit**; it **rejects** (unlike recruitment) |
| **Training** | **Improves knowledge, abilities and capacity** for the jobs |

**Significance:** **recognises competent staff** (number needed and placement); **enhances performance**; builds **ongoing capability** (**succession planning**); gives **optimal employment** of human resources (avoids under-utilisation); and raises **job satisfaction and morale**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Recruitment widens the pool; selection narrows it.

items.title: Systems approach to staffing and number of managers
items.core_explanation_md:
Staffing is an **open system** inside the company, linked to the **outside environment**, so it considers **internal factors** (**personnel policies, organisational climate, reward system**).

A **management inventory** compares **needs with available talent**; **internal and external sources** feed **recruitment, selection, placement, promotion and termination**; **performance review**, **career strategy** and **training** are also parts.

Staffing **affects leading and controlling**: trained managers build an atmosphere where members meet **enterprise and personal goals**; good managers **prevent big deviations**.

**Number and type of managers depend on:** **size of the business**, **complexity of structure**, **plans for expansion**, **turnover of managers**. No rule fixes the **ratio** of managers to staff; changing **delegation** can raise or lower the number. **Qualifications** of each manager must also be determined.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Numbers are only part of the picture: the fit of each manager to the role matters equally.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two factors affecting how many managers an organisation needs.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example size of the business and complexity of the organisation structure (also expansion plans and turnover).

items.title: Recruitment: stages and types
items.core_explanation_md:
**Recruitment** is **finding potential applicants and encouraging them to apply**; **staffing** is hiring the most qualified.

**Stages:** determine **need**; conceive a **strategy**; draft a **job description**; **publicise**; **recruit**; **examine applications**; **phone or initial screening**; **interviews**; **evaluate**; **background check**; **decision**; **references**; **offer**; **hire**; **on-board**.

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Internal** | Filling positions from **current staff** |
| **Retained** | A recruiting firm gets an **upfront fee** and an **exclusive** arrangement; **one firm per vacancy** |
| **Contingency** | The firm is paid **only when its candidate is accepted** |
| **Staffing agencies** | **Temporary or limited-time** jobs |
| **Outplacement** | **Employer-sponsored help** to **former employees** to find new work |
| **Reverse** | An employee is urged to seek a **better-fit employer** |

**Advice:** **look inside first**; contact **passive applicants**; **hire people already excelling** in similar jobs.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The difference between retained and contingency recruiting is when the recruiter is paid.

items.title: The selection process
items.core_explanation_md:
**Selection** is **choosing from a shortlist**. Steps (courseware):

1. **Preliminary interview** (excludes the unfit).
2. **Taking applications** (resume, cover letter).
3. **Examining applications** by a **screening committee**.
4. **Employment tests**: **IQ, aptitude, competence, personality**.
5. **Formal interview**.
6. **Verification of references**.
7. **Medical tests**.
8. **Final selection and appointment**: **appointment letter** with terms such as hours, pay and leave; often **on probation**.

**Importance:** the **company's success** rests on **careful selection and placement**; goals are achieved faster; **fewer industrial accidents** with the right technical staff; **satisfaction and output rise** when people do work they excel at; contented staff have **good morale**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware calls the formal interview the "fifth and last" step although three steps follow; the numbered list is taught.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Final selection and appointment (the appointment letter).

items.title: Training: importance, benefits and types
items.core_explanation_md:
**Training** follows orientation and **raises skills, capacities and knowledge** for particular jobs.

**Why:** new staff learn the **mission, vision, laws and working conditions**; existing staff **update skills**; to **keep pace with technology**; to **prepare for promotion**.

**Benefits:** **better morale** (less absenteeism and turnover); **less supervision**; **fewer accidents**; **better promotion chances**; **higher productivity**.

| --- | --- |
| **On-the-job** | **Learning by doing**: **job rotation, mentoring, temporary promotions**; **cost efficient** |
| **Off-the-job** | Away from the normal place of work: **workshops, seminars, conferences**; **costly** but good for **many people quickly**; **vestibule training** mimics real working conditions in a separate place |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Vestibule training is off-the-job training in a simulated work setting.

items.title: Retention and development of staff
items.core_explanation_md:
**Effective retention practices:** **accurate job preview at hiring**; **socialisation** (integration programmes); **training and development**; **compensation and rewards**; **fair supervision** (the **most critical factor** in staying, per studies); **employee involvement** (the courseware cites **engaged employees being five times less likely to quit**).

**Three compensation options:** be the **industry leader**; use a **person-based** structure; **link retention to rewards** (vacation hours by seniority, **retention bonuses**, **stock options**, defined benefit payouts by years of service).

**Strategies:** **comprehensive** (organisation-wide: hiring changes, working environment, **base pay by market rates**; data from **research, effective practices, benchmarking surveys**) and **directed at retention** (**exit interviews, post-leave interviews, stay interviews, focus groups, predicted turnover studies**).

**Implementation:** **lay the groundwork** (turnover analysis, benchmarking, needs assessment; plan; carry out; examine results); **external benchmarking** (compare with industry and competitors); **internal benchmarking** (track turnover over time).

**Common problems:** **no support from senior management**; the feeling that taking part is **pointless busywork**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A stay interview asks current employees why they remain, which helps prevent exits.

items.title: Knowledge management and the SECI model
items.core_explanation_md:
**Knowledge management (KM)** is **generating, exchanging, utilising and managing information and knowledge**.

**Benefits:** knowledge **supports products and services**; **shorter development cycles**; **creative endeavours**; use of **staff experience**; **problem solving**; managing **physical assets and intellectual property**.

**Technology:** **group-work software**, **workflow systems**, **content management**, **scheduling**, **electronic communication**; **e-learning or a learning management system (LMS)** is the base.

**SECI model (Nonaka and Takeuchi):**

| Stage | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ocialisation | **Constant flow of information** and **chat or interaction** among employees |
| **E**xternalisation | **Connecting online learning to real workplace events** |
| **C**ombination | **Regularly updating and streamlining training** using feedback and expert input |
| **I**nternalisation | Employees **absorb the knowledge** so they can **use skills immediately** |

Use **specific metrics** to judge an LMS; **managers' participation** is key.
items.expanded_explanation_md: SECI stands for socialisation, externalisation, combination, internalisation.

items.title: Performance appraisal: types, objectives, advantages and disadvantages
items.core_explanation_md:
**Performance appraisal** is the **periodic examination of an employee's contribution** (job performance and overall contribution); also called **annual review, performance review or evaluation**; usually **annual, semi-annual or quarterly**.

**Types:** **top-down** (manager); **self-evaluation**; **peer assessment**; **360-degree feedback** (self, supervisor and peers); **negotiated appraisal** (a **mediator**; the subject **presents first** to reduce the adversarial aspect).

**Objectives:** compare **actual with standard performance**; keep **records for pay and salary structure**; find **strengths and limitations** (placement); assess **potential**; give **feedback**; guide **training needs**; shape **approach to work**.

**Four purposes of use:** tell employees **how they are rated**; decide **merit raises**; decide **additional training**; decide **promotion**.

| **Advantages** | **Disadvantages** |
| --- | --- |
| Easier **promotion** decisions; **salary** input; staff **growth**; spots **training needs**; better **selection**; **communicates** performance; **inspires** | Elements may be **inaccurate or inappropriate**; may **gloss over** key aspects; **attitude and initiative** are **hard to evaluate**; **unqualified appraisers** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: In 360-degree feedback the employee, supervisor and peers all comment.

| **Rating scales** | **Numerical scales** on dependability, initiative, output, attendance, attitude | **Rater's bias** |
| **Trait analysis** | **Yes/no checklist** of traits | **Rater's bias**, **improper weights** |
| **Forced choice** | Rater **must choose** true or false in **blocks of statements**; HR assesses | Statements may be **wrongly framed** |
| **Forced distribution** | Employees **clustered around a high point** on the scale (**normal distribution** assumed) | Assumption **unrealistic**; **central tendency** errors |
| **Critical incidents** | Supervisors **record critical behaviours** as they occur | **Negative incidents prioritised**; **over-close supervision** |
| **Confidential records** | **Annual Confidential Report** (government departments) | **Secretive**, feedback only for **adverse entries**, **subjective** |
| **Pen portrait** | Assessor **writes a description** of the assessee (used for **army cadets**) | |

**Future-oriented methods:**

- **Management by objectives:** rate performance against **agreed objectives**.
- **Assessment centre:** **several evaluators** judge **situational exercises** (**in-basket**, **role-playing**, **critical incident**, **leaderless group discussion**), mostly for **first-level supervisors** and **promotion potential**; each candidate is rated **more than acceptable, less than acceptable or unacceptable**.
- **BARS (behaviourally anchored rating scales)**, five steps: **generate critical incidents**; **develop dimensions** (5 or 10 clusters); **reallocate incidents** (kept if **50 to 70 per cent** assign the same cluster); **scale the incidents**; **final instrument** with **6 or 7 incidents per dimension** as **anchors**. **Advantages:** **more accurate**, **clear standards**, **good feedback**, **independent dimensions**.

items.title: Key result areas and career strategy
items.core_explanation_md:
**Key Result Areas (KRAs)** are the **general areas of outcomes or outputs** a department or role is responsible for, derived from **short-term objectives**.

**Individual Performance and Development Plan** has two parts: the **Performance Plan** and the **Individual Development Plan**, built in **four steps:** (1) agree **key result areas**; (2) agree **performance objectives**; (3) agree **key performance indicators and their targets**; (4) agree **action plans**.

**Career strategy:** **informal appraisal** daily; **formal appraisals** once or twice a year. A **professional life plan** includes a **personal profile**, **long-range goals**, **risks and opportunities**, **strengths and weaknesses**, **strategic alternatives**, **consistency testing and choice**, **short-range objectives and action plans**, **contingency plans**, **implementation** and **monitoring**.

**Seven steps of a career development plan:** **analyse values, strengths and motivators**; **be aware of advantages**; **research possibilities**; **develop expertise**; **build a network**; **consider and evaluate alternatives**; **take action**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A KRA names an area of results; a KPI measures it and has a target.

items.title: Human resource development and managing generations
items.core_explanation_md:
**HRD** raises the **efficiency of individuals, groups and organisations** through **training, organisation and career advancement**.

**Benefits:** **more capable** people; **engagement**; a culture of **trust and respect**; **acceptance of change**; **teamwork**; an **efficiency culture**; **pride**; **data** that supports **planning**.

**Types:** **on-the-job training**; **work shadowing** (watching another do the work); **classroom or online education**; **professional growth** (university or certification courses, seminars).

**Managing generations: five best practices:** **do not make assumptions**; **avoid labels**; **review your own biases regularly**; **focus on the people around you, not on the trends**; **acknowledge and celebrate differences**.

**Diversity:** up to **four generations** (Baby Boomers to Generation Z) work together. **Advantages:** **problem solving**, **understanding diverse audiences**, **chances for educational growth**, **mentorship**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware warns that generational stereotypes lead to misunderstanding and can cost a firm good employees.

self_check.expected_takeaway: An employee watches another employee perform the duties to learn the necessary abilities.

items.title: Industrial relations, management of change and stress management
items.core_explanation_md:
**Industrial relations:** the **relations between labour and management** in industry: **employees and superiors**, **employees among themselves**, **union-management relations** and **relations among employers' associations, unions and government**. Healthy relations need **mutual respect, understanding, goodwill and acknowledgement of dignity**; **business cycles** matter (harmony in growth, strain in recession).

**Management of change:** manage the **conversation between those leading and those implementing change**, the **organisational context** and **emotional bonds**. Models cited: **Lewin** (**unfreeze, change, refreeze**) and **Kotter's 8 steps**. Change has **preparation, implementation and follow-through**. The manager must **understand the drivers** (**internal** pressures such as new leadership; **external** ones such as new technology or a competitor), **formulate a strategy**, **communicate clearly** to those affected and **be ready for obstacles**.

**Stress management:** treatments and **psychotherapies** to **regulate stress**, especially **chronic stress**; levels can be measured with **physiological tests**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Follow-through ensures a change is sustained and built into culture and practice.
